title: Stable decoupling: Three tests for Europe in the face of Chinese economic coercion – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Facing a €1bn-a-day trade deficit with China and the threat of critical-minerals retaliation, the EU must decide this autumn how to set rules for Chinese goods, investment and suppliers in critical infrastructure. Tobias Gehrke argues Europe should copy the US model of 'stable decoupling': accept narrow sectoral deals (e.g. on EVs) while keeping trade-defence, investment-conditionality and cybersecurity tools independent, and prepare for Chinese escalation.

insights.claim: The EU faces a trade deficit with China surging at €1bn a day alongside industrial deterioration across the continent and Chinese threats of economic coercion.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: The scale of the deficit makes tougher EU trade measures against China more likely, with implications for European industrials and Chinese exporters.
insights.quote: They are facing a surging EU trade deficit of €1bn a day, industrial deterioration across the continent and Chinese threats of economic coercion.

insights.claim: At a European Council summit in late October 2026, EU leaders will choose between negotiating a trade agreement with China or following a Franco-German push to unilaterally restrict China's access to the single market.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: The summit is a near-term catalyst for EU-China trade policy affecting autos, batteries and clean-tech equities.

insights.claim: Paris and Berlin's joint paper proposes new EU deterrence powers that would allow Chinese companies to be banned from the single market.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Franco-German alignment on hard tools raises the probability of escalatory EU measures against Chinese firms.
insights.quote: Their proposal for new deterrence powers, which would allow the banning of Chinese companies from the single market, is an important move.

insights.claim: In 2025 the US assumed big tariff hikes would force Chinese concessions, but China responded by expanding rare earth export restrictions, pressuring Western factories and defence production and forcing the White House to de-escalate.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Critical-minerals chokepoints give China effective escalation dominance over broad tariffs, a key risk for any Western trade offensive.
insights.quote: Instead, China responded by expanding restrictions on essential rare earth supplies. This put Western factories and defence production under immediate pressure.

insights.claim: The US is now pursuing stability and decoupling simultaneously, using targeted measures to restrict Chinese companies' market access beyond tariffs, curb Chinese investment and ban Chinese technology domestically.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Targeted decoupling rather than blanket tariffs is the emerging Western template, favouring non-Chinese suppliers in tech and infrastructure.
insights.quote: Despite China’s potent escalation options, the US is pursuing both stability and decoupling at the same time.

insights.claim: Compromise, autonomous action and escalation are not mutually exclusive for the EU: narrow sectoral accommodation with China can work as long as it does not impinge on Europe's broader economic security agenda.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Expect a dual-track EU policy: sector deals alongside continued trade-defence cases, so tariff-relief optimism should be narrow.

insights.claim: If the EU tackles Chinese trade, investment and infrastructure problems in a coordinated way, China will likely respond with coercive pressure, so Europe must accept and prepare for escalation.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Investors should price potential Chinese retaliation, including critical-minerals restrictions, against European manufacturers.

themes.theme: Trade: narrow EV deal vs broader distortions

insights.claim: A narrow EU-China trade settlement on automotive exports could see China voluntarily cap EV and hybrid shipments to the EU or expand 'price undertakings' with minimum import prices, volume limits or local investment commitments.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: A managed-trade EV deal would cap Chinese EV volumes in Europe and support pricing for European automakers.

insights.claim: Volkswagen Anhui, one of Volkswagen's China-based joint ventures, already agreed to EU price-undertaking market-entry terms earlier in 2026.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Price undertakings are already a working template for China-made EV imports, including by European OEMs.
insights.quote: Volkswagen Anhui, one of the German company’s China-based joint ventures, already agreed to such terms earlier this year.

insights.claim: A narrow car-focused deal would leave untouched other European sectors already under pressure from Chinese industrial policy, including batteries, wind equipment, robotics, machine tools, chemicals and biotechnologies.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: These sectors are candidates for future EU trade-defence actions and remain exposed to Chinese overcapacity.

insights.claim: The EU should retain the ability to launch anti-subsidy and safeguard investigations in other EV value-chain segments such as batteries, use anti-circumvention tools against rerouted Chinese exports, and apply the Foreign Subsidy Regulation and international procurement instrument across sectors.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Battery and other clean-tech imports from China face continuing trade-defence risk even if an EV deal is struck.
insights.quote: making a deal on one product cannot become a promise to tolerate distortions impacting on others.

insights.claim: The author proposes an EU diversification instrument, such as tariffs on overdependent imports, plus a strengthened anti-coercion instrument with a lower activation bar and a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by Chinese retaliation.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: New EU tools could force supplier diversification in critical sectors, benefiting non-Chinese suppliers.

insights.claim: Chinese investment in Europe including Britain recovered to almost €17bn in 2025, nearly a quarter of all Chinese FDI, with 45% of it in the automotive and EV sector.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Chinese EV makers are localising in Europe to bypass tariffs, adding competitive pressure on European automakers' home market.
insights.quote: reaching almost €17bn in 2025 (nearly a quarter of all Chinese FDI), with 45% of that investment in the automotive and EV sector.

insights.claim: China's exports are rising faster than its investment in Europe, driven by industrial policy support, persistently weak domestic demand and a weak yuan.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Weak Chinese demand and a weak yuan structurally push deflationary exports into Europe, pressuring margins in European manufacturing.
insights.quote: China’s exports are increasing at an even faster pace—supported by continued industrial policy support, persistently weak domestic demand and a weak yuan.
insights.locator: The problem for Europe is that

insights.claim: Without safeguards Chinese firms may set up 'screwdriver factories' in the EU that assemble pre-made components while keeping high-value activities in China, and Beijing has instructed its carmakers to follow this path and expanded control over which auto components may be exported.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Chinese EV plants in Europe may deliver little supplier-chain benefit to European component makers.

insights.claim: Under the proposed EU Industrial Accelerator Act, foreign investments above €100m in batteries, EVs, solar and critical raw materials would need to meet four of six conditions, but as drafted only local employment is mandatory, creating an 'à la carte' system.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: The final shape of investment conditions (JV, IP sharing, local sourcing) will determine how attractive EU market entry is for Chinese battery and EV firms.
insights.quote: Yet, as currently drafted, the only mandatory condition for foreign investors is to commit to local employment.
insights.locator: The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act

insights.claim: The author urges member states and the European Parliament to make more Industrial Accelerator Act conditions mandatory and extend it to industrial robotics, wind equipment and medical technology.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Investment conditionality could spread to robotics, wind and medtech, affecting Chinese entrants in those sectors.
insights.locator: It now falls to member states

insights.claim: Chinese companies still supplied nearly a third of 5G sites in 32 European countries in 2024 despite being designated 'high risk'.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Large legacy Chinese 5G footprints imply a sizable replacement market for trusted vendors if rules tighten.
insights.quote: Chinese companies still supplied nearly a third of 5G sites in 32 European countries in 2024, despite being designated as “high risk”.

insights.claim: Chinese-made solar inverters are connected to over 200GW of European solar capacity and supply 80% of newly installed inverters in Europe.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Inverters are a major grid-security exposure; restrictions would create demand for non-Chinese inverter makers.
insights.quote: Chinese-made solar inverters are connected to over 200GW of European solar capacity and supply 80% of all newly installed inverters.

insights.claim: Chinese state-owned COSCO holds stakes in multiple EU port terminals, ZPMC dominates global ship-to-shore crane production, and HMN Technologies has become the world's third-largest submarine cable supplier.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Ports, cranes and subsea cables are next in line for EU security scrutiny after 5G.

insights.claim: The revision of the EU Cybersecurity Act could extend the 5G high-risk supplier approach to connected equipment in ports, energy grids, connected vehicles and industrial control systems, assessing whether a supplier could be subject to foreign manipulation.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: A binding rulebook with replacement timetables and financing would drive a multi-year rip-and-replace cycle benefiting trusted equipment suppliers.
insights.locator: The ongoing revision of the EU Cybersecurity Act

insights.claim: Beijing has threatened consequences if the EU adopts security restrictions affecting Chinese companies, but trading national security autonomy for a limited trade truce would be a mistake, since China already pushes European technologies out of its own stack.
insights.speaker: Tobias Gehrke
insights.so_what: Security-based restrictions are unlikely to be traded away, so European tech access to China remains constrained regardless of trade deals.
insights.quote: But it would be a mistake for Europeans to trade their national security autonomy for a limited trade truce.
